13.0.s.en: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

13.0.0.en: 1 He who touches pitch is defiled, and he who keeps company with the proud becomes like him. 2 Do not lift a weight beyond your strength, and do not keep company with one who is stronger and richer than you. 3 How can an earthen pot be joined with a cauldron? If it is struck, it breaks. 4 The rich man does wrong and storms, and the poor man is wronged and entreats. 5 If you are useful, he exploits you, and if you are barren, he abandons you. 6 If you have money, he lives with you and drains your money, and he does not tire. 7 If he has need of you, he deceives you and smiles at you and promises you and speaks to you of good, and says: "What do you need?" 8 And he serves you food that shames you, until he drains your money two or three times, and finally he mocks you and sees you after that and abandons you, and shakes his head at you. 9 Humble yourself before God, and wait for His hand. 10 Beware of being deceived and humbled in your folly. 11 Do not be humbled in your wisdom, lest humiliation draw you into folly.

13.0.1.en: He who touches pitch is defiled, and he who keeps company with the proud becomes like him [1].

13.0.2.en: Most of the counsels in this book concern the young who have not yet enjoyed true spiritual experience, and who do not realize the danger of their clinging to some wicked friends, especially the rich among them.

13.0.3.en: Ben Sira presents an example, the young man who touches pitch, to confirm how dangerous defilement is through a sinful friendship; the pitch here is not the person of the friend nor wealth but evil and pride. His message is a warning to the young against certain categories of people, affirming that it is wise to avoid entering into friendships with them and clinging to them.

13.0.4.en: It is fitting for the believer to separate himself from the wicked in their evil conduct, and the places of their evil and deviations, so he avoids choosing the wicked as friends, in walking with them on the way and being absorbed with them in their thought.

13.0.5.en: v We read in the book of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus: "He who touches pitch is defiled by it" (see Sir 13:1). As long as we are occupied with the affairs of the world, as long as our souls are bound by possessions and money, we cannot think of God freely. "For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?" (2 Cor 6:14-15), says the Lord: You cannot serve God and mammon (Mt 6:24) [1].

13.0.6.en: St. Jerome St. Cyril the Great sees that the pitch that stains the soul is the gatherings that do not observe holiness.

13.1.0.en: v Now we must take care, we who have been justified in Christ and have enjoyed fellowship of the Holy Spirit through faith in Him, not to mingle with a people whose thoughts are perverted, of an unholy mentality. Such a people are in truth strangers, speaking a strange language, and speaking words perverted from the truth. Everyone who mingles with them is utterly defiled. Scripture says: "He who touches pitch is defiled" [2].

13.1.1.en: St. Cyril the Great Do not lift a weight beyond your strength, and do not keep company with one who is stronger and richer than you.

13.1.2.en: How can an earthen pot be compared with an iron cauldron?

13.1.3.en: The cauldron strikes it and it breaks [2].

13.1.4.en: The danger of friendship between a young man and a young man richer than he: that the poor young man is bound to keep up with the rich young man, as in exchanging gifts or banquets, so that the poor man finds himself obliged to spend what is beyond his means [2]. Sometimes a person is dazzled by his friend's wealth and tries to keep pace with him, and so is like an earthen pot that collides with an iron vessel and is shattered.

13.2.0.en: The rich man sins and proves himself the one wronged, and the poor man is wronged and is obliged to apologize [3].

13.2.1.en: A man's friendship with one who is richer than he exposes him to the shattering of his psyche, for the rich man sins and justifies the wrong he committed and his justification is accepted, while the poor man is wronged by the rich man, and is obliged to apologize to the wrongdoer.

13.3.0.en: If you are useful he (the rich man) exploits you, and if you are in need he abandons you [4].

13.4.0.en: If you have money he keeps company with you, and drains your money without feeling sorry for you [5].

13.4.1.en: It would be fitting for the rich man to thank God for His gifts by offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving through helping the needy, but some rich men, instead of supporting the needy, exploit them, as by offering them loans in return for high interest or usury. And in their selfishness, feeling that they have no need of the poor friend, they abandon him.

13.4.2.en: v When man does not put God before his face, what is before his eyes but the world? In other words he gathers money upon money, and is concerned to increase the flock, and his storehouses are filled, and he says to himself: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Lk 19:12).

13.4.3.en: v Rightly is the man sick with dropsy compared to the covetous rich man. The first, the more he receives unnatural moisture the more his thirst increases, so the covetous rich man who has received riches in abundance misuses them, and his passion for the love of wealth increases [3].

13.4.4.en: St. Augustine v Truly man's life does not consist in his possessions through the abundance he has, but he is counted blessed and with glorious hope who is rich toward God [4].

13.4.5.en: St. Cyril of Alexandria v The life of man does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses [5].

13.4.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v If you offer to God a part of what you acquired unjustly and by seizure, He will not accept your gift... Have mercy on him you have wronged, showing him mercy and love... For God does not share in our greed, nor does He share with thieves and robbers; He is able to feed the poor whom He entrusted to us, but He seeks the fruits of righteousness and love of people.

13.4.7.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic v "He labors in vain and without profit, he who clings to the wealth which he will not taste" (Job 20:18) LXX. What is the use of the splendor of a palace dripping with gold if the wicked man himself is buried six feet beneath (the earth)? What is the use of an abundance of garments of joy and a variety of clothing for a person whom the vermin strip?

13.4.8.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem v Does wealth make you live longer? Why then do you show evils for the sake of an unsure comfort?

13.4.9.en: Father Theophylact v We must know that covetousness sometimes steals into people by way of pride, and sometimes by way of fear. Therefore some aim at appearing with greater authority, and burn to obtain what belongs to others. Also there are people who fear lest they come to be in want of the necessities of life, so they give their minds over to covetousness to seek what belongs to others, imagining that what they have is not enough for them.

13.5.0.en: If he has need of you he deceives you, and smiles at you, and gives you hope and speaks to you of good, and even says: "What do you need?" [6]

13.5.1.en: He shames you with his foods, until he drains you two or three times, and finally mocks you.

13.6.0.en: And if he sees you after that he forgets you, and shakes his head at you [7].

13.6.1.en: Ben Sira calls us to flee from the table of the wicked, for while he offers you food and drink he does not carry within him true love, but what occupies him is the cost of the table he offered you, or how to exploit the offering of the banquet to push you to evil. The wise man says: "Do not boast before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men: for better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen" (Prov 25:6-7). The Lord Christ gives us counsel at invitations to banquets, saying: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; And he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have glory in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Lk 14:8-11). It is fitting for the believer to be adorned with self-control and comprehensive chastity: chastity of the belly, and chastity of the hand and tongue and senses.

13.7.0.en: Beware lest you be led astray, and be humbled in your folly [8].

13.8.0.en: 12 If a powerful man invites you, withdraw; for thereby he will increase his invitation to you. 13 Do not push forward, lest you be driven away, and do not stand far off, lest you be forgotten. 14 Do not venture to converse with him, and do not trust his many words; for by his much speaking to you he tests you, and by smiling at you he examines you. 15 He is without mercy. He does not carry out what he promised, and does not refrain from harm and fetters. 16 Be on your guard and take great heed; for you are on the brink of falling. 17 And if you hear these things in your sleep, wake up. 18 In all your life, love the Lord and call upon Him for your salvation.

13.8.1.en: If a ruler invites you, be slow in accepting the invitation, for often he will increase his invitation to you [9].

13.8.2.en: Do not press him, lest you be rejected, and do not withdraw, lest you be forgotten [10].

13.8.3.en: Do not intend to converse with him as his equal, and do not trust the abundance of his words, for he tests you by much talk, and while he smiles he examines you [11].

13.8.4.en: Ordinarily there is an innate sensitivity in man toward one who is his peer, that is, equal to him in age or education or work. For man deals with compassion with one who is younger than he without being jealous of him, and also with one who is older than he without resentment, because his age gives him the right to precede him. Ben Sira warns the poor young men not to speak much, and not to disclose their secrets before the rich young men and those in authority.

13.8.5.en: He who does not guard your words is without mercy, and does not hesitate to harm you or imprison you [12].

13.9.0.en: Keep your words to yourself and take heed, for you are walking on the brink of your fall [13].

13.10.0.en: 19 Every living creature loves its like, and every man loves his neighbor. 20 Every creature keeps company with its kind, and a man associates with his like. 21 Does the wolf associate with the lamb? So is the sinner with the godly. 22 What peace is there between the hyena and the dog? And what peace is there between the rich and the poor? 23 Wild asses in the wilderness are the prey of lions, and so the poor are the pastures of the rich.

13.10.1.en: God gave most beings to love what resembles them. By this nations and tribes were formed, as a people live together and sympathize with one another because of unity of language and similarity of color and culture. And in the kingdom of animals we see them going out together: lions walk together in one herd, and so do leopards and bears and deer, and we do not find a lamb grazing among wolves or foxes, nor a cat among snakes or a dove flying in a flock of ravens. So we are not surprised to see groups of one kind of bird flying together and also migrating together, and in the migration of fish, fish of a certain kind set out together. But in the Church of the New Testament, human beings sympathize together not on the basis of unity of language or color of skin or culture, but the heart of the believer is enlarged, sympathizing with the children of men, longing that all become the icon of God and that the whole world become "a holy nation" (1 Pet 2:9); that is, the one Kingdom of God.

13.10.2.en: Every living creature loves what resembles it, and every man loves his neighbor [14].

13.10.3.en: v God planted in our nature an attraction that binds us to one another by love. "Every beast (creature) loves its own kind, and every person loves his neighbor" (see Sir 13:15). Behold, there are in our nature seeds that incline us to virtue; while the seeds of vice are contrary to nature. If the latter are dominant, this is nothing but a testimony to our extreme sluggishness [6].

13.10.4.en: v We all by nature adopt a friendly attitude, so we feel indignation with those who are treated with contempt... and we sympathize with those who enjoy help and protection, and are overcome by the trials that befall others, as we have a common tenderness. For although painful events seem as though they drive to a kind of cowardice, yet we harbor a kind of common tenderness. One speaks of this, explaining: "Every living creature loves its own kind, and every man loves his neighbor" [7].

13.10.5.en: St. John Chrysostom v "Every creature loves its own kind, according to the saying: "People seek to be united with those like them." It seems very desirable even among us to live with those who have the same habits as we, so how can we escape the thought that this is the case with God? For being good by nature, and the beginning of all virtues and their source, He takes up His dwelling not in lovers of evil, but in doers of virtue, and rises above defilement [8].

13.10.6.en: St. Cyril the Great In a sermon of Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, on the feasts of the holy martyrs, he sees that celebrating the holy martyrs is realized in practice by fellowship with them and by imitating their conduct, as the wise man says: "Every creature loves its own kind" (see Sir 13:14).

13.10.7.en: v As we desire to celebrate the feasts of the holy martyrs, the blessed martyrs want to recognize some of their virtues in us, so that they may be pleased with us and seek God's mercy on our behalf... For like keeps company with like, and what is not like withdraws far from it. Look at our holy patron, whose feast we zealously want to celebrate rejoicing; he is self-controlled, so how can a drunkard keep company with him? What fellowship is there between a humble soul and a proud soul [9].

13.10.8.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles Every body associates according to its kind, and every man clings to him who is like himself [15].

13.10.9.en: The goal of dealing with those of our kind is not jesting and amusement but our eternal salvation.

13.10.10.en: v Do not talk with just anyone about mercy and the virtuous life. And I do not say this out of envy, but because I reckon that you will be in the eyes of the fool like a jester. A man agrees with one who resembles him, and the hearers of such (spiritual) talk are few, or rather very rare, so it is better not to speak, for (mere talk with them) is not what God wants for the salvation of man [10].

13.10.11.en: St. Anthony the Great What harmony is there between a wolf and a lamb?

13.10.12.en: So is the sinner with the godly man [16].

13.10.13.en: What peace is there between the hyena and the dog?

13.10.14.en: And what peace is there between the rich and the poor? [17]

13.10.15.en: Wild asses in the wilderness are the prey of lions, so the poor are the pastures of the rich [18].

13.10.16.en: Sirach turns to the world of animals to illustrate the grave contrast between kinds of people, for in the animal world they devour one another. The wolf devours the lamb [17]. There is nothing the lamb can offer to remedy the wolf's attitude toward it except to flee from his company. At the same time, on the positive side, wealth itself is not evil, but the evil lies in man's thought and his wicked will.

13.10.17.en: Since sin entered the world, even some irrational creatures were corrupted. The strong lion does not cease to devour animals weaker than he, such as wild asses. And the rich exploit the poor and count them their pasture. Ordinarily we do not find the poor man dwelling beside the rich man, because the rich man often exploits the poor man, and by one means or another lays his hand on what the poor man owns, if he does not also lay his hand on the poor man himself! As King Ahab and his wife Jezebel did with Naboth the Jezreelite (1 Kgs 21), taking away his vineyard, and the queen devised a plot to kill Naboth. A very few control the great positions of leadership, while the price is paid by the poor; so the rich grow richer, and the poor poorer.

13.10.18.en: v They do not care about righteousness; instead, looking to (their own) profit, they tyrannized over the needy, to profit from the wretched and use them as sandals (Amos 8:6). Scripture says: "The poor are the pastures of the rich" [18]... Love of neighbor is bound up with the accomplishments of righteousness, for truly "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour" (Rom 13:10) [11].

13.11.s.en: 4. Between the rich and the poor

13.11.0.en: 24 Humility is an abomination to the proud, and so the poor man is an abomination to the rich. 25 When the rich man is shaken, his friends hold him up, and when the humble man falls, his friends drive him away. 26 The rich man slips and many help him. He speaks outrages and they acquit him. 27 The humble man slips and they rebuke him. He speaks with sense, and they give his words no place. 28 The rich man speaks and all listen, and they lift his speech to the clouds.

13.11.1.en: Ben Sira sees the danger of the great disparity among people in regard to wealth and power, especially if society lacks true wisdom.

13.11.2.en: The proud man loathes lowliness of station, and so the poor man is an abomination to the rich [19].

13.11.3.en: The proud man sees in humility uncleanness, and at the same time sets himself up as a god, so he becomes like the Antichrist who claims divinity, and sets up the abomination of desolation in the temple.

13.11.4.en: If the rich man totters his friends support him, and if the poor man falls his friends push him [20].

13.11.5.en: When the rich man is exposed to stumbling (tottering), he relies on his wealth and his friends to offer him help. But the man of God finds in God Himself and His rich grace the true help and heavenly comfort that penetrates his depths.

13.11.6.en: v I reckon that a life passed in fellowship with some persons in the same dwelling is more useful in many respects. The reasons for this are: first, none of us is self-sufficient with regard to material needs, but each one asks the help of another to meet our needs. The foot, for example, has one kind of strength and lacks another. And without cooperation with the other members of the body it finds itself unable to carry on its activities independently of the others for a long time... So in the life of solitude, what is in the hand becomes of no use to us, and what we do not have we cannot achieve, since God the Creator ordained that we must help one another as it is written, so that we may be gathered together [12].

13.11.7.en: St. Basil the Great When the rich man slips many help him, and when he speaks wicked words they acquit him.

13.11.8.en: If the poor man slips they rebuke him all the more, and when he speaks with understanding no place is given to him [21].

13.11.9.en: If the poor man falls no one supports him, but his friends push him down all the more to be rid of him. This is what happened with the Lord of glory Jesus at His trial, so that His disciples might not wait for help or praise from people.

13.11.10.en: When the rich man speaks everyone is silent, and they lift his word to the clouds.

13.11.11.en: And the poor man speaks and they say: "Who is this man?", and if he stumbles they push him down all the more [22].

13.12.s.en: 5. Wealth is good for him who uses it well

13.12.0.en: 29 The poor man speaks and they say: "Who is this?" And if he stumbles they overthrow him. 30 Wealth is good for one who has no sin, and poverty is hateful in the mouth of the hypocrite. 31 A man's heart changes his countenance, either for good or for evil. 32 A cheerful countenance comes from a good heart, and the devising of proverbs wearies the thoughts.

13.12.1.en: Wealth in which there is no sin is good, but poverty is evil in the mouth of the wicked [23].

13.12.2.en: Lest anyone suppose that all the rich are wicked or harsh or exploiters of the poor, he made clear that wealth is good for him who uses it well, and ugly for him who misuses it. If a man's face sometimes bears a sweet smile and attractive features when the heart is pure, and sometimes bears marks of violence and harshness or anger when the heart is angry, so it is with wealth.

13.12.3.en: Is wealth a sin? What occupies the believer is the sanctification of his heart, which is reflected even in his features.

13.12.4.en: v Let us all teach our children to prefer virtue to anything else, and not to give importance to material wealth... Abraham was rich and so was Job; these two not only suffered no harm from wealth, but also enjoyed a good reputation... because they did not use it for their own enjoyment alone, but also for the comfort of others, relieving the pains of need, and opening their house to every stranger [13].

13.12.5.en: St. John Chrysostom St. Anthony the Great calls us to the moderate life.

13.12.6.en: v The more a man is moderate in his life the more he is at peace, for he is not full of concern for many things, such as servants and hired hands and sheep... Yet when we cling to such things we become exposed to the troubles that flow from them, which lead us to murmur against God.

13.12.7.en: And so the passion that springs from our own will (to acquire many things) fills us with disturbance, and we flounder in the darkness of the life of sin, not knowing ourselves [14].

13.12.8.en: St. Anthony the Great A man's heart changes the features of his face, either to good or to evil [24].

13.12.9.en: With Ben Sira's concern for man's inner life, and his warning against judging a man by outward appearances, he affirms that the inner life has its effective influence on man's outward features. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the joy that man's features bear is only a reflection of the peace of the heart. It is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" (Prov 15:13).

13.12.10.en: A cheerful face is a sign of a heart full of goodness, but devising proverbs requires laborious thought [25].

13.12.11.en: How great the difference between a man who records maxims and proverbs quoted from the words and writings of others, and one who records them as the fruit of an experience he lives out in his thought and conduct. Therefore Ben Sira, who has tested the upright life in the Lord, says: "Devising proverbs requires the labor of thoughts."

13.12.12.en: v He also says: "Your face is beautiful." You can understand what kind of "face" this is that the word of God praised and described as beautiful, if you understand what Paul meant by the face in his saying: "But we all, with open face beholding..." (2 Cor 3:18), and his saying also: "but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). It is without doubt a kind of face that is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), after the image of its Creator (Col 3:10), having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but being holy and without blemish, like the Church that Christ presents to Himself (Eph 5:27).

13.12.13.en: In other words it means the souls that have reached perfection, those that form the body of the Church; this body appears truly beautiful and handsome when the souls of which it is composed persevere in obtaining the beauty of perfection. For just as the soul, when it is in turmoil, distorts the shape of the bodily face and makes it agitated, while if it is calm it gives the face a shape that bears peace and gentleness, so also the face of the Church is beautiful or ugly according to the traits of the believers and their aspirations.

13.12.14.en: It is written that the cheerful face points to a prosperous heart [25], and in another place it is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the countenance is broken" (Prov 15:13). The heart is joyful when the Spirit of God is in it, whose first fruit is love, and the second is joy (Gal 5:22). And I think that the worldly wise have taken their ideas from these truths, since they said that the wise man is beautiful, and every wicked man is ugly [15].

13.13.s.en: Let me lean on Your breast, not the breast of a man!

13.13.0.en: v Your breast, O Savior of the world, is wide enough for every man!

13.13.1.en: You are the humble rich One; every humble man cleaves to You!

13.13.2.en: Grant me not to lean on a rich man nor on one in authority.

13.13.3.en: He may welcome me, but I do not know what is in his heart toward me.

13.13.4.en: But You are all love, You pour out of Your riches and Your grace into my heart.

13.13.5.en: v Many of the rich were drawn by money, and they have friends who honor them for their wealth and authority.

13.13.6.en: When they stumble many hasten to support them.

13.13.7.en: And when they sin, people flatter them, and justify their errors.

13.13.8.en: But I in my weakness cleave to You, for You truly love me and help me.

13.13.9.en: Reveal Your presence in my depths, that I may meet Your heavenly servants and the company of the saints.

13.13.10.en: In You I am enriched and never in want of anything!

13.13.11.en: v He who forms a friendship with a wicked, proud rich man is like one who touched pitch and was defiled.

13.13.12.en: And he who forms a friendship with You, his heart is lifted up to Your heavens.

13.13.13.en: The devil dares not creep in to him, nor set his snares for him on the way.

13.13.14.en: With every morning he enters into new glories, and his soul rejoices in his journey in Your company.

13.13.15.en: You overshadow him, and protect him from the sun of trials.

13.13.16.en: And by Your Holy Spirit he flies as on the wings of an eagle.

13.13.17.en: He is not taken to the Promised Land as happened of old, but You carry him to the heavenly Canaan, and the heavenly orders marvel at him and call him blessed.

13.13.18.en: He who keeps company with the wicked rich man becomes wicked like him.

13.13.19.en: He who keeps company with You, O Holy One, finds sweet the union with You!

13.13.20.en: v Clinging to the rich is a burden on the poor.

13.13.21.en: They suffer from them, and are broken as the earthen pot is broken by the metal vessel.

13.13.22.en: And clinging to You offers him sweetness, for Your yoke is sweet, and Your burden is very light.

13.13.23.en: v Clinging to the wicked rich exposes the poor man to injustice.

13.13.24.en: And by clinging to You he enjoys Your righteousness, and enters into Your depths through the wounds of Your love.

13.13.25.en: Your cross has become a divine chariot that carries us and sets out with us to You without hindrance.

13.13.26.en: v Clinging to the wicked rich man exposes me to his withdrawing from me.

13.13.27.en: He abandons me and counts me a stranger to him.

13.13.28.en: I feel isolation and suffer from deadly loneliness.

13.13.29.en: But clinging to You, O Holy One, makes me a member of Your holy body.

13.13.30.en: I meet You face to face, and enjoy the Fatherhood of the Father and the sanctification of Your Holy Spirit.

13.13.31.en: I shall never feel isolated as long as I am in Your presence.

13.13.32.en: And I find sweet the fellowship with the heavenly ones and the saints.

13.13.33.en: v My soul will not be at rest when a powerful ruler invites me.

13.13.34.en: He may invite me once and twice, but what, I wonder, does his heart hold toward me?

13.13.35.en: If I sit at his table I will not look at the splendid food, for I cannot keep pace with him in his temporal wealth.

13.13.36.en: And if he speaks to me with a smile, I do not know whether he truly loves me or is testing me.

13.13.37.en: But You, O heavenly Bread, offer me a heavenly table.

13.13.38.en: You do not send me manna from heaven, as You did in the wilderness.

13.13.39.en: But You came down to me offering me Your holy Body and Your precious Blood.

13.13.40.en: By them I receive from Your hands the fellowship of the divine nature.

13.13.41.en: You grant me the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy and peace, goodness, meekness and chastity, wisdom, understanding and discernment.

13.13.42.en: O Your surpassing, free table that satisfies my heart and my mind and all my depths!

13.13.43.en: In truth I become like You, and am a living icon of You.

13.13.44.en: v My depths cry out to You:

13.13.45.en: My tongue is unable to express the power of friendship with You, and the blessedness of the mystical fellowship with You, O You who are wonderful in Your love and Your friendship.
